"A hundred," he repeats. "Easy." He looks at Fred, and Fred's grin has gone wide and slightly dangerous.

"Right," Fred says. "First batch of each design stays with us — for testing. Every product gets tested before it sells, that's the rule, and it's *your* name on the rune work." George leans back. "And we should probably talk about the *paper shortage* story, because if we're raising prices, we need a reason people will believe."

cases.narratorContent:
Fred's doing the maths on his fingers.

"Twenty-four of each, four designs, that's ninety-six units. At three galleons a low end —" he whistles. "That's two hundred and eighty-eight galleons. In a *week*." He looks at George. "We made forty selling rubbish to first years all last year."

"Because we were selling rubbish," George says. "These are different." He looks at you. "Twenty-four's a good number. Enough to look like supply, not enough to flood the market. And we're sold out of twelve already — that's word of mouth doing its job."

Fred leans in. "Question is which one we lead with. The Liar's the flashy one. Everyone wants to catch someone out." He pauses. "But the Placebo Confidence one's the real genius, because it's free to make, does nothing, and people will *swear* it works."

Fred calculated 96 units at three galleons minimum as roughly 288 galleons a week, against last year's forty. George endorsed 24 as enough to look like supply without flooding the market, noting the twelve already sold were generating word of mouth. Fred noted the liar-detection design is the flashy lead and the placebo confidence design is nearly free to make. The plan is agreed in principle for tomorrow, not yet executed.
